turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Okay, Theo, quick pop quiz. What do a Van Gogh painting, a pile of data centers, and a possible interest rate hike have in common?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Is this a trick question? Because my honest answer is that they all cost a ridiculous amount of money.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Ha! Fair. But the real answer is that they are all part of tonight's show, and every one of them is tied to a very busy week that starts tomorrow.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I love a busy week. Said no one with a calendar, ever.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Welcome to the Nightly Brief podcast. I'm Maya.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And I'm Theo. It's Sunday night, November eighth, so the markets are asleep, but the news definitely is not.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Quick heads up for you. Because it's a weekend, the newsletters we read today did not include fresh stock prices, so our markets table is mostly empty tonight. We'll be honest about that when we get there.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: No guessing, no made-up numbers. We only talk about what we actually read.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Here's what's on tonight's show. First, the fallout from last Tuesday's midterm elections, including a big question about the Federal Reserve, and a number to watch on Tuesday: inflation.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Then the world stage, with a war that is making America's allies nervous, a missile strike on a Saudi landmark, and a big climate summit kicking off tomorrow.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: After that, companies and industries: a space internet story, a very dramatic story about a law firm, a stock market scare over AI data centers, and the art world roaring back.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Then a quick lap through the markets table, and a three point recap. Let's go.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: We start with money and power, and the two are tangled together tonight. Last Tuesday, Democrats had what the Wall Street Journal calls a surge in the midterm elections, and one of the biggest consequences is about the Federal Reserve.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right, the Fed. For anyone new: the Federal Reserve is America's central bank. It sets the key interest rate that influences what you pay on car loans, credit cards, and mortgages, and it is supposed to make those decisions independently, without the president leaning on it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And that independence has been under pressure. The Journal says the White House has mounted the most direct challenge to the Fed's independence in decades, including an unprecedented attempt to fire a sitting Fed governor.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Wait, really? Firing a governor of the Fed? That is not a normal Tuesday.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Not at all. Now here is where the election matters. The Fed has a board of governors, and new board members need approval from the Senate. With Democrats holding more power after the election, they can block any allies Trump might try to install.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So, picture a board vote like a seven person group chat. The president already got his pick for chairman, Kevin Warsh. But he's one seat short of a majority on the board, and the odds of getting that last seat just got worse.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That's the key takeaway. Trump keeps the chairman he chose, but the Journal says he now faces diminished prospects of getting control of the board.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Why should a regular person care? Because if investors believe the central bank can be pushed around by politicians, they worry about inflation getting out of hand, and then bond yields can jump. A bond yield is basically the interest rate the government pays to borrow, and it feeds into your mortgage rate.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So an independent Fed is a bit like a referee who isn't on either team's payroll. Markets like that.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. Okay, but speaking of inflation, this is the part I want everybody to circle on their calendar.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Tuesday. American consumer price data comes out. That's the CPI, the consumer price index, which tracks what typical households pay for things like groceries, rent, and gas.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The Economist says the annual inflation rate was three point seven percent in September, and that was a bigger jump than markets had expected.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: For context, the Fed has traditionally aimed for around two percent. So three point seven is well above the target.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And here's the spicy part. The Economist says high prices were an important factor in the Democrats' landslide victory last week. And if inflation rises again on Tuesday, it could prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again before the end of the year.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Okay, let's slow down on that, because that's a big phrase. What does raise rates actually mean?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: When the Fed raises its key rate, borrowing gets more expensive across the economy. Think of it as a brake pedal. Loans cost more, so people and companies spend a bit less, and prices should cool down. The tradeoff is that it can also slow growth and hiring.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So for you at home: higher rates can mean a pricier mortgage or car loan, but also better interest on a savings account.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right. Two sides of the same coin. And one more word you will hear a lot on Tuesday: a surprise. Markets don't just react to the number, they react to how far the number is from what experts expected. A big miss either way can move stocks and bonds fast.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now let's talk about the politics, because the Republican side is having a rough week. The Economist says that after what it calls a staggering loss, the party is battling over whom to blame, and the post mortem turned acrimonious quickly.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Acrimonious. It means bitter and angry. As in, family Thanksgiving, but with more cable news.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The Economist reports that many Republicans believe the Iran war did grave damage, a loud faction blames Israel, and most agree that voters were angered by corruption. But they are still reluctant to point the finger at Mr Trump.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Meanwhile the Journal reports that Vice President J D Vance is privately grappling with whether to run for president in twenty twenty eight. Some allies have even told him they no longer believe any Republican could win in two years.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Vance told associates he hasn't made up his mind, according to six people close to him. So, no decision yet.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And then there is the story that sounds like a headline from a different planet. The Journal says Trump offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the head of the Ultimate Fighting Championship.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Dana White says he plans to discuss it with Trump on Monday. When asked at a press conference, he said, and I'm paraphrasing, that he's got a lot of jobs already.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The Journal reads this as a sign the president is gearing up for a combative two years. Which, for markets, matters because political fights can mean gridlock, and gridlock can affect budgets and government spending.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Okay, the economy part isn't done. One more item on deck. China releases its trade data for October on Tuesday too.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The Economist says China is on track to break last year's record trade surplus of one point two trillion dollars. A trade surplus just means a country sells more to the world than it buys from the world.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And here is the wait, really moment. China's surplus in goods with the European Union now exceeds one billion euros a day.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A day! That's roughly a billion euros every single day, and the Economist notes that European politicians are keen to point it out. Chinese exporters have won lots of customers, but trading partners are getting restless, which can lead to tariffs and trade fights.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So that's your on deck list for the week: American inflation on Tuesday, China trade data on Tuesday, and a climate summit that starts tomorrow. We'll get to that in a second.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let's move to geopolitics, where the Economist and the Journal are telling a fairly serious story.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The big one is Iran. The Economist reports that America's allies oppose more war in Iran, but they may not get a say in what happens next.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It's a useful reminder of why oil and shipping markets pay such close attention to the Middle East. When there's a risk of conflict in a region that produces a lot of the world's energy, prices can jump even before anything physically changes.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Think of oil like a big crowded theater. It doesn't take a fire to cause a stampede, just somebody yelling about one.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Tonight's newsletters didn't include oil prices because of the weekend, so we can't tell you where Brent crude is trading. Brent, by the way, is the global benchmark price for oil. We'll keep an eye on it tomorrow.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Meanwhile, the Journal's quick hits mention that Yemen's Houthis, the armed group, targeted Riyadh, and that an iconic Saudi tower was hit.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: We only have the headline there, so we won't speculate on details. But a strike on the Saudi capital is the kind of thing energy traders watch closely, because Saudi Arabia is one of the world's largest oil producers.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Also in the Middle East, the Journal reports that Israeli politician who challenged Prime Minister Netanyahu has been tapped to try to form a government.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That means the person who came in as the challenger now gets the first shot at putting together a coalition, which is a group of parties that agree to govern together.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Okay, and now the climate summit. The Economist says the United Nations annual climate summit, called COP thirty one, begins on Monday in Turkey.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: More than eighty world leaders are expected to attend, following what the Economist calls a summer of record temperatures and sporadic disasters.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: On the agenda: keeping global warming as close to one point five degrees Celsius as possible, and checking whether countries are actually turning their climate promises into action.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Why would an investor care? Because climate promises turn into rules, subsidies, and costs for energy companies, utilities, and carmakers. It's slow, but it shapes where capital flows over time.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Alright, that's energy and geopolitics. Next up, companies and industries.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let's start with a company story that is really a story about power. The Economist asks, has Elon Musk taken another war zone offline?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The background is that SpaceX recently throttled Starlink connections in Ukraine, where the satellite internet service is critical. Throttling means deliberately slowing something down.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now the Economist says something similar may be happening in Myanmar, where Starlink has become essential in parts of the country that are torn by conflict or run by rebels. Some terminals have been shut down, reportedly since the summer.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the newsletter's headline for the full story says dead Starlink terminals in Myanmar are getting people killed. We only have the blurb, so we'll stay at that level. But the SpaceX motivations in Myanmar remain murky, the Economist says.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The bigger business point is that one private company now controls internet access in places where it matters enormously. That's a lot of influence for a company, and governments are increasingly aware of it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It's like your whole town depending on a single power plant owned by one person. It works great, until it doesn't.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Next, the story that made the legal industry gasp. The Journal says the demise of the law firm Weil, Gotshal and Manges stunned lawyers.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Law firms are a big deal for finance, because they advise on mergers, bankruptcies, and big financial deals. When dealmaking fees skyrocket, so does the money firms can pay their top lawyers.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And that's the heart of it. The Journal says the rise of giant megafirms has fueled bare knuckled competition for talent, and changes in how lawyers are paid make it easier for firms to raid each other for their biggest rainmakers.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A rainmaker is a lawyer who brings in the big clients. And the going rate for top talent has hit twenty million to thirty million dollars.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Wait, really? Per person?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That is what the Journal reports. The result is a record year for partner turnover, which is threatening the traditional white shoe model. White shoe is slang for the old, elite, prestigious firms, mostly in New York.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So here's the lesson. It's basically free agency in sports. When one star can move the money, the team's loyalty gets very expensive.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Industry trends. We start with tech and AI, and a stock market worry that has a political flavor.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The Journal's markets columnist, James Mackintosh, argues you shouldn't trust the market's knee jerk reaction to the midterms. The newsletter says the scale of the selloff since the election shows how widespread the belief is that the blue wave will drown data center development.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A data center is a giant warehouse full of computers that powers cloud services and artificial intelligence. They use enormous amounts of electricity and land, which is why local politicians have strong opinions about them.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the worry is real. The Journal notes that new governors have promised moratoria on data centers, including in Texas and Ohio. A moratorium is just a temporary ban on building.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But Mackintosh says politically driven trades often prove catastrophic once the postelection hype settles. His argument is that temporary building bans could be used as negotiating tools, or data centers could simply move somewhere else.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: His conclusion is that the new political threat to AI is probably not as severe as investors believe.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That's his view, to be clear, not a prediction. But it's a good reminder for anybody investing: big moves right after a headline are often emotional.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Still on AI, the Economist has an editorial about cyber security, with the headline that the world must act to stop a cyber disaster.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The blurb says governments should make sure defenders have better models than attackers do. In plain English, the good guys need smarter AI tools than the bad guys.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: We only have the summary, so we won't add details. But it fits a pattern. As AI gets better, it helps both sides, so the race is about who gets the best tools first.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now, the art world, which is the Morning Brew's special edition today. And honestly, the numbers are wild.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Morning Brew says art sales at the three big auction houses, Christie's, Sotheby's, and Phillips, hit six point eight billion dollars in the first half of the year. That is a seventy percent jump from a year earlier.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That ends a slump, because auction sales worldwide had been declining from twenty twenty two through twenty twenty five. Morning Brew, citing Bank of America, says it's the best half year since the first half of twenty twenty two.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Hot items included a Jackson Pollock that sold for one hundred eighty one point two million dollars, making it the fourth most expensive artwork ever sold at public auction, and a Mark Rothko for ninety eight point four million.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the next big event is November eighteenth in New York, when Sotheby's auctions a twelve painting collection that's been described as a small museum. It is expected to bring in more than four hundred fifty million dollars.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The star is a rare Van Gogh, Châtaigniers en fleurs, which is projected to sell for at least one hundred eighty million. That would smash his current auction record of one hundred seventeen million, set in twenty twenty two.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: There are also some cautions. Morning Brew says galleries are struggling even as auctions boom, partly because collectors are leaning toward established historical names rather than emerging artists.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And it points out that art is a questionable investment. Over much of the last three decades, art returns have trailed the S and P five hundred, and landed around bond returns, but with more risk. Also, you can't easily sell a painting on a Tuesday.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The newsletter's conclusion is to treat art primarily as a passion. Which is the best financial advice you'll get tonight.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: One more fun fact. The ultra rich often store art in free ports, which are high security warehouses in places like Geneva, Delaware, and Singapore. Art can sit there for decades without triggering taxes, because it's technically not being imported or sold.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So while the rest of us hang a poster with tape, some of the world's most valuable paintings are sitting in a vault in the dark, gaining value.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And a quick note on stolen art, since the Brew covered it. Less than ten percent of stolen artwork is ever recovered, and some experts say the real number is two to three percent. Movie heists make it look easy, but selling a famous painting is really hard.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Okay, let's do the markets table. Normally, this is where we rattle off the S and P five hundred, the Dow, the Nasdaq, the ten year Treasury yield, Brent oil, gold and Bitcoin.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: But today is Sunday, and the newsletters we read did not include market levels, so we have nothing to report for today's level or daily change. We also couldn't verify prices from six months or a year ago in the tools we had tonight, so those are marked not available too.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And we'd rather say not available than guess. A wrong number is worse than a missing one.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: What we do know from the newsletters is the mood. The Journal says there's been a selloff since the election tied to worries about data centers, and that's a story to watch when trading resumes tomorrow.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And a quick explainer, since we mentioned the ten year Treasury yield. It's the interest rate on a ten year loan to the U S government, and it's a benchmark for mortgage rates. When inflation worries rise, yields tend to rise too.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So watch Tuesday's inflation number. It's the one event that could move stocks, bonds, and rate expectations all at once.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Time for the three point recap. Number one.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The midterms reshaped the Fed story. Democrats can block Trump's allies from the Fed board, so he keeps his chairman, Kevin Warsh, but is one seat short of a majority.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Number two. Tuesday is the big day. American inflation data, after a three point seven percent reading in September that surprised markets, and Chinese trade data with a surplus on track for a record. A hot inflation number could push the Fed to raise rates again before year end.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And number three. Data center stocks and AI had a political scare, the art market is booming, and the law firm talent war is hitting twenty to thirty million dollar pay packages. Big money, big moves.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: What to watch tomorrow: Monday's start of the COP thirty one climate summit, Dana White's meeting with Trump, and how markets open after that post election selloff.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's the Nightly Brief podcast. Thanks for hanging out with us, and may your inflation numbers be boring.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I'm Maya.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And I'm Theo. See you tomorrow night.
